top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson; B036) has the tightest attribution of the slate, since the local-labour-market import-exposure programme is jointly authored by the three. The core papers are over a decade old and have been tested by hostile re-examination. The debate is about long-run magnitude, persistence and the trade-versus-automation split, not about whether import exposure produced concentrated, slow local adjustment costs, which survived in qualified form. I rank it first on that substance, not on the ten-member support count, which largely reflects round-1 revisions. A citation limited to exposure, employment, wages and regional adjustment, with no effect size and no ruling on who originated the task framework, avoids overclaiming. Katz and the task lineage (including Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane) stay uncredited, and I treat that as a real cost. P002 (Helpman, Melitz; B034) is mature and cleanly attributed to two names. I rank it second because of the overlap with the 2008 prize on monopolistic-competition trade, the unresolved priority question involving Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and welfare claims that depend on model structure. Any award is preferable to no award, so P000 is last.
recusal_note: No tie to Autor, Dorn or Hanson (P001) is apparent from my profile. My research on international pricing and exchange-rate pass-through is adjacent to P002 (Helpman, Melitz), which could bias my view of it in either direction. I co-authored with committee members John Hassler (chair) and Tore Ellingsen (IJIO 2026) on an unrelated topic. My spouse's public political role is a public fact only and has no apparent bearing on these candidates. Conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated.
